prompt.context: Our client is a 350-bed hospital in a mid-size city. The organization has historically exhibited strong financial performance, and had a 1-3% operating gain each year for the last five years. However, they are projecting a $12 million operating loss this year, and expect this situation to worsen in the future. As a result, the CFO believes that they will be out of cash within five years. They have asked us to identify the source of this sudden downturn, and to come up with alternatives to restore them to a break-even position. They are one of the largest employers in the market, and will not consider layoffs as a possible solution.
prompt.question: What is causing the hospital's financial downturn, and what alternatives would you recommend to restore the hospital to a break-even position?

clarifying_info.a: Revenues have dropped approximately 15% so far this year due to aggressive pricing on capitated managed care contracts signed in January and declining admissions and length of stay for fee-for-service contracts, most of which are still reimbursed on a per diem basis. All contracts are binding for three years and cannot be renegotiated.

clarifying_info.q: What is driving cost increases or cost issues?
clarifying_info.a: The utilization of diagnostic and therapeutic services during a patient's stay is approximately 15% higher than what was expected when contract pricing was negotiated.

clarifying_info.q: What does the local competitive market look like?
clarifying_info.a: There are two other 350-bed hospitals in the city — one is an academic medical center, the other a Catholic hospital recently acquired by a for-profit chain. Total admissions in the marketplace have dropped by 5% and total patient days have declined 10%.

framework: Revenue side: analyze managed care contract pricing, fee-for-service reimbursement rates, admissions volume, and length of stay
Cost side: distinguish fixed vs. variable costs; identify that staffing (layoffs excluded) and resource utilization are key variable cost drivers
Identify root causes: revenue locked in by 3-year contracts at aggressive prices; variable costs (resource utilization) running 15% over plan
Generate alternatives: revenue enhancement strategies AND cost reduction strategies, plus structural/competitive options

questions.prompt: What are the root causes of the $12 million projected operating loss?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies both sides of the profit equation. On revenue: contracts were priced too aggressively (capitated) and fee-for-service volume is down (admissions and length of stay declining). On costs: resource utilization (diagnostics, therapeutics) is 15% above the level assumed in pricing — creating a double squeeze. Candidate should note that revenue is effectively fixed for 3 years (contracts not renegotiable), making cost management the short-term lever.

questions.prompt: Given that layoffs are off the table and contracts are locked in, what cost reduction levers remain?
questions.guidance: Focus on variable costs tied to resource utilization, which physicians ultimately control. Strong answer covers: (1) Align physician incentives with hospital financial goals — share risk, provide comparative utilization data and education vs. peers/competition. (2) Purchasing/supply chain — sign exclusive distributor contracts for volume discounts; limit pharmacy formulary to generics; reduce vendor count for high-volume items (e.g., prosthetics, heart catheters). (3) Operational efficiency in utilization of diagnostic and therapeutic services.

questions.prompt: What revenue enhancement strategies could the hospital pursue?
questions.guidance: Despite locked contracts, candidate should brainstorm new revenue streams: (1) Sign contracts with additional insurers not currently contracted. (2) Hire salaried physicians on staff to guarantee admissions flow to the hospital. (3) Create an affiliated physician organization to capture a larger share of admissions. (4) Develop Centers of Excellence leveraging distinctive competencies — market these to managed care contractors as exclusive regional providers, potentially attracting out-of-region patients.

questions.prompt: Are there any structural or market-level solutions worth considering?
questions.guidance: Given market context (2 other 350-bed hospitals; total admissions down 5%, patient days down 10%), candidate should consider: affiliate or merge with a competitor to rationalize capacity city-wide, potentially allowing one hospital to close. This reduces fixed costs across the market, improves utilization at remaining facilities, and rationalizes service offerings across institutions.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible ways the hospital could restore itself to break-even, given it cannot lay off staff and its contracts are fixed for three years?

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Resource Utilization
ideas: Change physician ordering behavior through incentive alignment and risk-sharing
Provide physicians with comparative utilization data vs. peers
Limit pharmacy formulary to generic drugs only
Reduce number of vendors for high-volume items (prosthetics, heart catheters)
Negotiate exclusive distributor contracts for volume discounts

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement — Existing Operations
ideas: Sign contracts with additional insurers not currently in network
Hire salaried physicians to guarantee admission volumes
Create affiliated physician organization to increase admissions market share
Develop and market Centers of Excellence to managed care contractors as exclusive regional providers

categories.name: Strategic / Structural
ideas: Affiliate or merge with a competitor hospital to rationalize city-wide capacity
Rationalize service lines across institutions to reduce duplication
Seek to close one hospital in the market, reducing fixed costs sector-wide
Explore out-of-region referrals for specialized Centers of Excellence

recommendation: In the short term (within the 3-year contract window), focus on reducing variable costs by changing physician behavior through incentive alignment, comparative data sharing, and supply chain consolidation (formulary restrictions, exclusive distributor contracts).
In the medium term, pursue revenue growth by adding insurer contracts, building an affiliated physician organization, and developing Centers of Excellence to capture incremental managed care volume.
Structurally, explore affiliation or consolidation with one of the two other 350-bed competitors to rationalize market capacity and reduce fixed costs across the city.
risks: Physician resistance to incentive changes or utilization restrictions may limit cost savings
Consolidation with a competitor (especially the for-profit chain) may face regulatory or cultural obstacles
Centers of Excellence require upfront investment before generating revenue
New insurer contracts may also be priced aggressively in a competitive market
next_steps: Quantify the gap: model how much cost reduction is needed to reach break-even given the 15% revenue decline
Conduct physician utilization analysis to identify highest-impact targets for behavior change
Assess feasibility of affiliation or merger with the Catholic/for-profit hospital
Identify which service lines have the strongest competitive position to anchor a Centers of Excellence strategy
